title: Nth Fibonacci Number
description: Given n, print the nth Fibonacci number with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1.
intendedApproachSummary: Use memoization or tabulation so each Fibonacci state is solved once.
wrongApproachHints: Plain recursion repeats work exponentially.
This is the standard first DP state-reuse example.
hints: F(n) depends on F(n-1) and F(n-2).
Store solved values.

examples.explanation: The Fibonacci sequence is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.

title: Climbing Stairs
description: Given n stairs, print the number of distinct ways to climb to the top when you can take 1 or 2 steps at a time.
intendedApproachSummary: Ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). This can be solved with a small rolling state.
wrongApproachHints: This is Fibonacci-shaped; a full exponential recursion is unnecessary.
hints: Start from the smallest stair counts.
Only the last two answers are needed.

examples.explanation: The 5 ways come from different 1-step and 2-step combinations.

title: House Robber
description: Given money in houses along a street, print the maximum money you can rob without robbing two adjacent houses.
intendedApproachSummary: At each index, choose between skipping the house or taking it and skipping the previous one.
wrongApproachHints: Greedily taking the larger immediate house can fail.
This is a take-vs-skip recurrence.
hints: State i depends on i-1 and i-2.
Memoization or tabulation both work.

examples.explanation: Rob houses with values 2, 9, and 1 for a total of 12.

title: Maximum Sum of Non-Adjacent Elements
description: Given an array, print the maximum possible sum of elements such that no two chosen elements are adjacent.
intendedApproachSummary: Fill dp[i] as the best answer up to index i using take or skip logic.
wrongApproachHints: This is closely related to House Robber but with general integers.
hints: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], arr[i] + dp[i-2]).

examples.explanation: Choose 3, 7, and 12.

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
description: Given the cost of stepping on each stair, print the minimum cost to reach just beyond the top when you may climb 1 or 2 steps at a time.
edgeCases: Starting from either stair 0 or stair 1
intendedApproachSummary: The minimum cost for stair i depends on the cheaper of the previous two states plus cost[i].
wrongApproachHints: Greedy local choice does not always lead to the optimal total.
hints: You can start from index 0 or 1.
Only the last two costs are needed.

examples.explanation: Start at stair 1, pay 15, and jump to the top.

title: Unique Paths
description: Given an n x m grid, print the number of unique paths from top-left to bottom-right when you may move only right or down.
outputFormat: Print the number of unique paths
intendedApproachSummary: Each cell gets paths from the top cell and left cell.
wrongApproachHints: Brute force recursion is too slow for bigger grids.
hints: Initialize the first row and first column carefully.
Transition is dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1].

examples.explanation: There are 28 distinct right/down paths.

functionContract.javaSignature: public int uniquePaths(int n, int m)

title: Minimum Path Sum
description: Given an n x m grid of non-negative integers, print the minimum path sum from top-left to bottom-right when moving only right or down.
intendedApproachSummary: DP state at each cell is its value plus the smaller of top and left path sums.
wrongApproachHints: Greedy local choice is not enough because future path costs matter.
hints: Use a large sentinel for unavailable directions.
This can be reduced to one rolling row.

examples.explanation: The minimum path is 1 -> 3 -> 1 -> 1 -> 1.

title: Subset Sum Equal to Target
description: Given an array and target sum K, print Yes if a subset sums to K, otherwise No.
intendedApproachSummary: Take-or-skip DP over index and current target.
wrongApproachHints: This is not a greedy pick-largest-first problem.
Every item has a skip branch too.
hints: Base: target 0 is always possible.
Transition from previous row or smaller target.

examples.explanation: Subset 4 + 5 reaches 9.

title: 0/1 Knapsack
description: Given weights, values, and capacity W, print the maximum value obtainable by taking each item at most once.
intendedApproachSummary: For each item, choose between not taking it or taking it if capacity allows.
wrongApproachHints: This is 0/1 knapsack, so an item cannot be reused.
A ratio-based greedy method is not correct here.
hints: Transition from previous item row.
Take branch uses capacity - weight[i].

examples.explanation: Taking items 20 and 30 yields the best value 220.

title: Coin Change Minimum Coins
description: Given coin denominations and an amount, print the minimum number of coins needed to make the amount, or -1 if impossible.
outputFormat: Print the minimum number of coins or -1
intendedApproachSummary: DP over amounts where dp[x] is the best answer using all available coin choices.
wrongApproachHints: Greedy biggest-coin-first fails for many coin systems.
Use a large sentinel for unreachable states.
hints: Try every coin as the last coin used.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description: Given an array, print the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
intendedApproachSummary: dp[i] stores the LIS ending at i. Extend from previous smaller values.
wrongApproachHints: A contiguous subarray is not the same as a subsequence.
Initialize every dp[i] to 1.
hints: For each i, check all j < i.
If nums[j] < nums[i], try dp[j] + 1.

examples.explanation: One LIS is 2, 3, 7, 101.

title: Longest Bitonic Subsequence
description: Given an array, print the length of the longest subsequence that first increases and then decreases.
outputFormat: Print the longest bitonic subsequence length
intendedApproachSummary: Compute LIS ending at each position and LDS starting at each position, then combine them.
wrongApproachHints: You need two DP passes, not one.
Subtract 1 when combining because the peak gets counted twice.
hints: Run LIS left to right.
Run LIS-like logic right to left for decreasing part.

examples.explanation: One bitonic subsequence is 1, 2, 10, 4, 2, 1.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
description: Given two strings, print the length of their longest common subsequence.
edgeCases: One string fully contained as subsequence
intendedApproachSummary: Build dp over prefixes. Match characters by taking diagonal + 1, otherwise take the best of top and left.
wrongApproachHints: Substring and subsequence are different.
You need an extra base row and column.
hints: If chars match, use dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.
Else take max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

examples.explanation: ace is a common subsequence of length 3.

functionContract.javaSignature: public int lcsLength(String a, String b)

title: Edit Distance
description: Given two strings, print the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and replacements required to convert the first string into the second.
intendedApproachSummary: Use DP over prefixes with transitions for insert, delete, and replace when characters differ.
wrongApproachHints: Do not confuse this with LCS directly; the operations have explicit costs.
hints: Base row/column represent converting to or from empty strings.
If chars match, carry the diagonal value.

examples.explanation: horse -> rorse -> rose -> ros.

functionContract.javaSignature: public int editDistance(String word1, String word2)

title: Matrix Chain Multiplication
description: Given matrix dimensions arr where the ith matrix has size arr[i-1] x arr[i], print the minimum scalar multiplications needed to multiply the full chain.
intendedApproachSummary: DP over intervals. For every chain [i, j], try every split k and keep the minimum total cost.
wrongApproachHints: Multiplying from left to right greedily is not always optimal.
Interval length order matters.
hints: Transition uses dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j].

examples.explanation: The best parenthesization yields cost 26000.

title: Frog Jump with K Distance
description: Given heights of stones in a line, a frog starts at index 0 and wants to reach index n - 1. From any stone i, it may jump forward by 1 to k positions. The cost of a jump from j to i is abs(heights[i] - heights[j]). Return the minimum total energy needed to reach the last stone.
edgeCases: k can be larger than the current index
Several previous jumps may give the same minimum energy
intendedApproachSummary: Let dp[i] be the minimum energy to reach stone i. Try every valid previous jump length from 1 to k and take the minimum dp[i - jump] + abs(heights[i] - heights[i - jump]).
wrongApproachHints: A greedy jump to the closest or cheapest immediate stone can fail later.
This is not a fixed two-state recurrence because each index may have many valid predecessors.
hints: For each i, inspect all previous positions from i - 1 down to i - k.
Keep the best transition cost among those reachable predecessors.

examples.explanation: One optimal route is 10 -> 20 -> 25 with total cost 10 + 5 = 15.

functionContract.javaSignature: public int frogJumpKDistance(int[] heights, int k)

title: Reach Last Stone with Jump Memory
description: Given a sorted array stones of stone positions, a frog starts on stones[0]. The first jump must be exactly 1. If the last jump was k, the next jump may be k - 1, k, or k + 1, but it must stay positive. Return true if the frog can reach the last stone, otherwise false.
outputFormat: Print true if the last stone is reachable, else false
edgeCases: The second stone must be at position 1
A reachable stone may still fail if the jump history is wrong
The same stone can be revisited conceptually with different last-jump lengths
intendedApproachSummary: Use memoization or state caching on (stone index, last jump length). From each state, try jumps of k - 1, k, and k + 1 if positive, and continue only when that next position exists in the stones set.
wrongApproachHints: Tracking only whether a stone is reachable is not enough because future options depend on the last jump size.
This is not the same as minimizing jump cost over a fixed local window.
hints: The state needs both the current stone and the last jump length.
Use a map from stone position to index or reachable jump sizes.
Skip next jumps that are 0 or negative.

examples.explanation: One valid jump sequence is 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5.

title: Stock Profit with Cooldown
description: Given daily stock prices, you may buy and sell as many times as you like, but after selling you must wait one full day before buying again. Return the maximum profit.
edgeCases: Cooldown blocks an otherwise tempting immediate rebuy
Best answer may involve multiple separated trades
intendedApproachSummary: Model states such as hold, sold, and rest for each day, or use memoization on (day, holding, cooldown). Transition carefully so selling today enforces a cooldown before the next buy.
wrongApproachHints: This is not the same as unlimited transactions with no waiting period.
A greedy local buy-sell pair can block better future profit because of the cooldown.
hints: Think about what information from today determines what is legal tomorrow.
Holding, just sold, and resting are enough to describe the state.

examples.explanation: The best sequence respects the cooldown and yields total profit 3.

title: Knight Stay Probability
description: On an n x n chessboard, a knight starts at (row, col). On each move it chooses uniformly among the 8 standard knight moves. Return the probability that the knight remains on the board after exactly moves moves.
inputFormat: Four integers n, moves, row, col
outputFormat: Print the probability as a decimal value
edgeCases: Small boards lose probability mass quickly
Only in-bounds transitions contribute to the next state
intendedApproachSummary: Let dp[move][r][c] be the probability of being at cell (r, c) after move steps. Distribute each state equally across the 8 knight moves, skipping moves that leave the board.
wrongApproachHints: Do not treat this like a shortest-path count problem; probabilities add, not minimums.
Out-of-bounds moves do not contribute further probability.
hints: Start with probability 1 at the initial square.
Each legal outgoing move contributes one-eighth of the current probability.

examples.explanation: Only a small fraction of the knight's random paths stay on the board for both moves.

title: Stock Profit with Two Transactions
description: Given daily stock prices, return the maximum profit using at most two complete transactions. You may not hold more than one stock at a time.
edgeCases: Zero profit when prices never rise
Using fewer than two transactions can still be optimal
The state must know whether a transaction has already been consumed
intendedApproachSummary: Track day, holding status, and how many sells remain, or compress to the named states first buy, first sell, second buy, and second sell.
wrongApproachHints: Taking the two locally best disjoint intervals greedily can fail.
The recurrence must distinguish holding from not holding and account for the transaction count.
hints: What states do you need after the first buy, first sell, second buy, and second sell?
Selling is the action that completes a transaction.

examples.explanation: Buy at 0 and sell at 3, then buy at 1 and sell at 4.

title: Reach Bottom-Right with Obstacle Eliminations
description: Given a grid of 0s and 1s, start at the top-left corner and move only right or down. You may eliminate at most k blocked cells marked 1. Return true if you can reach the bottom-right corner, otherwise false.
inputFormat: Three integers rows, cols, and k
rows lines each containing cols space-separated 0/1 values
outputFormat: Print true if the destination is reachable, else false
edgeCases: The starting or ending cell may itself consume budget if blocked
A cell can be reachable with one budget value and unreachable with another
Large k may make many paths viable
intendedApproachSummary: Use DP on row, column, and used budget. A state is reachable if either the top or left predecessor can reach it while paying the current cell's obstacle cost without exceeding k.
wrongApproachHints: Tracking only whether a cell is reachable is not enough because different remaining budgets lead to different futures.
Do not spend budget twice for the same cell transition.
hints: The state needs both position and budget spent or remaining.
For a blocked cell, only predecessor states with one extra budget unit available can continue.
Right/down only keeps the problem DP-friendly.

examples.explanation: Eliminate one blocked cell in the middle column and continue to the destination.

functionContract.javaSignature: public boolean canReachWithObstacleEliminations(int[][] grid, int k)

title: Maximum Non-Adjacent Sum After Point Updates
description: Given an integer array and q point updates, after each update compute the maximum sum of a subsequence such that no two chosen elements are adjacent. Return the sum of all q answers.
inputFormat: q lines each containing index and newValue
outputFormat: Print the sum of the maximum non-adjacent subsequence answer after every update
edgeCases: Negative values mean the empty subsequence may still be optimal
A single update can affect the answer across a large range
The merge must forbid selecting adjacent boundary elements from neighboring segments
intendedApproachSummary: Build a segment tree where each node stores enough DP state to describe whether its left and right boundaries are selected. After each point update, merge updated nodes upward and read the root answer in O(log n).
wrongApproachHints: Recomputing a full House Robber DP after every update is too slow for large q.
A segment summary that stores only one best value cannot merge correctly across adjacency boundaries.
hints: Think of each segment as exposing multiple boundary states, not one scalar answer.
When merging two child segments, the left child's right boundary and the right child's left boundary cannot both be selected.
Point updates only change one leaf, so a segment tree can rebuild the answer efficiently.

examples.explanation: After updating index 1 to 2, the best non-adjacent sum is 12. After updating index 0 to -1, the best sum is 9. The total is 21.

functionContract.javaSignature: public long sumMaxNonAdjacentAfterUpdates(int[] nums, int[][] updates)
